memory_leads.lead: Liner commercial roles separate beneficial cargo owner/shipper, freight forwarder, NVOCC and ocean carrier: an intermediary may buy carrier space and sell logistics or transport commitments onward without owning the vessel.

A rate quotation or indication is a commercial offer state rather than a confirmed carriage state; validity, route/service basis, equipment assumptions and ancillary charges can change before booking.

Booking requests and carrier confirmations form a distinct capacity-commitment state machine: requested cargo, equipment, origin/destination and sailing may be accepted, amended, rejected, rolled or cancelled before loading.

Contracted allocations or space commitments can reserve commercial access to capacity separately from the physical vessel slot pool; allocation utilization, under-use and over-demand shape who actually gets space in tight markets.

Service-contract/longer-term rate arrangements and spot bookings allocate price and volume risk differently; realized carrier mix depends on actual lifted volumes, allocation use and contemporaneous market conditions rather than one benchmark rate.

Base ocean freight and surcharge/accessorial components can be separately quoted, triggered or revised, so invoice economics may diverge materially from a headline freight rate; exact tariff names and legal applicability are deferred.

Rolling a booking to a later sailing, blanking/cancellation effects, customer no-shows and late cargo create commercial capacity leakage between confirmed bookings and loaded containers, complicating both utilization and customer reliability.

Freight forwarders can consolidate cargo, coordinate inland legs and documentation, while NVOCC-style intermediaries may issue their own transport documents and procure underlying ocean carriage; exact licensing/legal distinctions vary by jurisdiction.

Bill-of-lading or sea-waybill style documentation is a downstream state from booking: shipping instructions, draft review, issuance/release and corrections can affect cargo release and commercial closure even after physical loading.

Documentation and cargo cutoffs create operational-commercial deadlines: missing shipping instructions, verified weight or other required data can break the path from booked cargo to accepted load even if space and equipment exist.
Equipment release links the commercial booking to P017's physical box pool; a confirmed booking can remain unusable until the correct equipment is released and collected at an actionable location.

Freight payment, credit approval, prepaid/collect allocation and invoice-dispute states can affect document/cargo release and counterparty exposure; exact credit terms and local practices are deferred.

Post-booking customer-service work—amendments, schedule-change notices, rollovers, document corrections and charge disputes—forms an administrative layer that can preserve or destroy the value of nominal service capacity.

Container indices versus realized liner economics require a contract-mix bridge: spot/contract share, customer mix, allocation utilization, surcharges and actual lifted volume can all separate reported revenue per unit from a public benchmark.

Effective liner capacity is commercially rationed as well as physically constrained: network slots, equipment pools and customer allocations jointly determine whether a shipper can actually secure carriage.
Counterparty risk extends beyond carrier solvency to shipper/forwarder credit and payment chains, especially when an intermediary owes one party while collecting from another.

Known-time replay should distinguish rate quote, booking confirmation, later roll/schedule notice, document issuance and final invoice timestamps because the commercial state evolves after the initial booking decision.
The broad distinction between container spot indices and contract benchmarks is already explicit in the atlas index-semantics lead; P018 only adds the booking/allocation bridge to realized revenue.

Equipment scarcity and inland/port bottlenecks as effective-capacity constraints are already covered by the atlas and P017; P018 retains only how they alter booking acceptance and commercial fulfillment.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Exact carrier contracts, tariff codes, surcharge names/amounts and route applicability require dated Evidence and would become a directory.
Document vocabulary is useful orientation but title, carriage, release, liability and jurisdictional effects require claim-scoped Evidence.
Blind recall cannot support exhaustive company histories, licensing status or jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction distinctions.
Carrier/customer practices and contractual thresholds differ by period, trade and counterparty and require Evidence.

stop_reason: The liner commercial interface is populated from quotation and booking through allocation, equipment release, documentation/B/L and invoice/payment states; further recall becomes carrier-, customer-, tariff-, route-, form- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no carrier contract, tariff, surcharge, allocation, booking, document legal effect, credit term or historical commercial outcome is verified.
